title: Observable-Level Framework for Finite-Key Security in Coherent-One-Way Quantum Key Distribution
authors: Aryan Kuntal, Utkarsh Giradkar, Mudit Chaudhary, Amit D. Lad
abstract: Practical security analysis of Coherent-One-Way (COW) quantum key distribution requires optical-device modeling, finite experimental statistics, and security inference to be treated consistently without conflating assumptions. We present a modular observable-level simulation framework organized through the pipeline θ_phys -> p -> O -> S_j(O), in which physical source, channel, receiver, and detector parameters determine detector-resolved event probabilities, a finite-block layer applies an effective dead-time treatment and generates aggregate detector counts, and interchangeable security evaluators act on the same observable record. The framework is verified against analytical optical, virtual-state, and finite-key relations and evaluated against reported experimental COW-QKD operating points. The Kato finite-key calculation reproduces the refined experimentally reported secure-key rates most closely at intermediate distances, with deviations of -1.5% at 50 km and -10.3% at 75 km. Monitoring bright-port decoy counts agree within 0.9-2.4%, while remaining distance-dependent dark-port residual identifies the principal model-sensitive observable of the present physical description. Applying Kato and Azuma-Hoeffding concentration treatments to identical detector records isolates the effect of finite-key statistical inference and shows substantially tighter Kato phase-error bounds for rare-event monitoring records studied here. Holding the Kato evaluator fixed, joint optimization of coherent-state mean photon number mu and receiver splitting fraction t_B increases model-predicted secure-key rate by 7.4-20.2% relative to optimization of mu alone with t_B = 0.3. The framework therefore provides a common computational interface for experimental reproduction, controlled security-model comparison, model-based protocol optimization, and modular adversarial stress testing in COW-QKD.
summary: This paper presents a novel, modular, observable-level simulation framework for analyzing the finite-key security of Coherent-One-Way QKD. By separating physical modeling, statistical counting, and security evaluation, the authors provide a robust tool for comparing theoretical security bounds with real-world experimental measurements. The framework allows for controlled optimization and stress-testing against various eavesdropping attacks.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for a consistent framework to analyze finite-key security in Coherent-One-Way (COW) Quantum Key Distribution (QKD). It aims to treat physical modeling, finite experimental statistics, and security inference separately to avoid conflating assumptions.
main_result: The developed observable-level framework successfully reproduces key rates close to experimental reports at intermediate distances, and joint optimization of key parameters ($\mu$ and $t_B$) significantly boosts the predicted secure-key rate.
method: The authors developed a modular, three-stage simulation pipeline ($\Theta_{phys} 	o p 	o O 	o S_j$) that maps physical parameters to observable counts, which are then analyzed using advanced concentration inequalities like Kato's and Azuma-Hoeffding.
model_or_system: The system analyzed is the Coherent-One-Way (COW) QKD protocol, which uses weak coherent pulses. The model is a computational framework that simulates the entire process from physical source parameters through detector-resolved event probabilities to final security estimates.
key_observables: Detector-resolved event probabilities, aggregate detector counts ($\mathbf{O}$), empirical gains ($\mathbf{b}_{Qd}$), Z-basis bit-error rate ($\mathbf{E}_z$), and the phase-error upper bound ($\mathbf{E}_u^p$).
important_parameters: Coherent-state mean photon number ($\mu$), receiver splitting fraction ($t_B$), channel loss, and the block size ($N$) used for finite-key estimation.
main_assumptions: The framework assumes that the physical modeling, finite-key statistics, and security evaluation can be treated as distinct, modular steps. Virtual gains must be bounded using experimentally accessible decoy statistics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the layered architecture, comparisons between finite-key treatments (Kato vs. Azuma-Hoeffding), and the dependence of the secure-key rate on optimization parameters ($\mu$, $t_B$) and adversarial perturbations ($p_{IR}$, $q$).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the observable-level pipeline, verifies it against analytical relations, demonstrates the use of concentration inequalities for finite-key analysis, and finally applies the framework to optimize key rates and test against representative eavesdropping attacks.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, computational interface for testing quantum communication protocols against realistic experimental constraints, which is crucial for advancing practical quantum networking technologies.

FIG. 2. Secure-key-rate comparison against experimental benchmarks. The discrete markers denote the refined exper- imental secure-key rates reported by Cao et al. [18]. The Cao-compatible asymptotic, Kato finite-key, and Azuma– Hoeffding finite-key results are evaluated using the corre- sponding reported operating parameters at each distance. The Gao asymptotic result is evaluated separately as an op- timized reference under its own state-preparation convention and therefore does not constitute a like-for-like reproduction of the experimental operating points. Azuma–Hoeffding re- sults are shown only at operating points for which the adopted finite-key bound certifies a positive secret key.

FIG. 3. Controlled same-record comparison of finite-key phase-error estimation. The phase-error upper bound EU p is evaluated as a function of the coherent-state mean photon number µ at (a) 25, (b) 50, (c) 75, and (d) 100 km. At each (L, µ) point, the Kato and Azuma–Hoeffding finite-key eval- uators receive the identical detector-resolved record O; their separation therefore reflects only the statistical security treat- ment. The Gao asymptotic result is included as a reference.
